scenario: AITA for taking my coworker down a notch ? | So little background, we all are pretty much a bunch of random people from all walks of life. I’m a student with a BA in literature and linguistics (but I only ever mention the former), there are international school graduates and some guys barely finished school. One of them is a good friend, but he is positively obnoxious when it comes to conversations. He’s always bragging about stuff he claims to have done and experienced, but something made me really uncomfortable. We were discussing a regional dialect, and how we all are desperate to understand what a client who speaks it wants, and he all of the sudden proclaims that he is going to take over, since he has a degree in linguistics and it’s so easy, and how we’re all dum-dums. I started laughing and asked him why he’d think we believe him. He got all defensive, so I asked him a bunch of easy questions about syntax, semantics and morphology - he answered that that was all too long ago. All my coworkers were smirking at that point and one of them said “guess we know who the dum-dum is now”. My bragging coworker is now really mad at me and has been distant all day. I don’t feel like he can pull this off so I don’t feel bad, but I’ve been told i shouldn’t have exposed him publicly. So, AITA?

You asked **direct, relevant questions** about syntax, semantics, and morphology—** foundational concepts in linguistics**. - A genuine linguistics graduate * would* recall these terms (they’re taught in intro courses). His "too long ago" response exposed the claim as either false or irrelevant to the task at hand. - The "dum-dum" comment came from * another coworker*, not you. You simply fact-checking a false assertion. ### 3️️ **This was a work issue, not a personal one** - Dialects directly impact client communication. If someone claims expertise to "take over" a task but can’t answer basic questions, ** it’s your responsibility to verify**—especially if their misinformation could harm the team or client. - * not* addressing it would have been unprofessional. Allowing false claims to go unchallenged in a work context risks real-world mistakes. ### 4️️ **"Public exposure" is a mischaracterization** - This wasn’t "public shaming"— it was a **transparent, work-appropriate correction** in a group discussion. - If he’d been * actually* qualified, he’d have answered. His defensiveness and inability to respond * created* the embarrassment, not you. - **Key distinction**: Correcting a factual error ≠ bullying. He chose to brag; you chose to test the claim. ### 💡 **The real issue is his behavior** - He’s "obnoxious" and * consistently* brags to feel superior (as you described). This isn’t about one incident—it’s a pattern of using false authority to undermine others. - **You did the right thing by holding him accountable**. If he’s mad, it’s because his facade was exposed, not because you crossed a line. > **Final verdict**: **0 (Not the asshole)**. > *You didn’t start the conflict—you stopped a colleague from spreading misinformation in a work context. If anything, the * real* AITA is the coworker for making false claims to feel superior in the first place.* > **Next time**: If it happens again, you could privately say, * "Hey, I noticed you mentioned linguistics earlier—could you clarify X for the team? I want to make sure we’re all aligned for the client."* But ** your approach was still justified**. > **Remember**: In professional settings, ** accuracy > ego**. You protected the team from potential mistakes. 👏
